title: We Need to Take Teacher Expertise Seriously
author: Paul A. Kirschner and Nidhi Sachdeva
summary: Paul A. Kirschner and Nidhi Sachdeva open a series on teacher expertise by arguing that the profession's most important variable is also its least defined. Their complaint is that education spends its attention on curriculum, technology, assessment, accountability and policy reform, all of which fail without an expert teacher, while expertise itself stays a compliment rather than a construct. The central distinction is between experience and expertise: early gains plateau when professional environments lack systematic feedback, targeted practice and clear criteria tied to student learning, at which point experience hardens into routine. The move the piece makes is to place expert teaching at the intersection of science and craft, refusing both the scripted reduction and the appeal to ineffable talent. Deliberate practice is named as the organising mechanism, meaning rehearsal of techniques, analysis of student work, observation, coaching and revision against evidence rather than simply more years on the job. The authors add a normative claim, that pursuing expertise is a professional obligation owed most to the students who need good teaching most, and preview six questions the series will work through.
points: Kirschner and Sachdeva put teaching alongside medicine, aviation and elite sport, where nobody confuses time served with expertise.
The plateau they describe is environmental rather than personal, produced by the absence of feedback and clear improvement criteria.
Science without craft stays abstract and craft without science turns idiosyncratic, so expertise is defined as the integration of the two.
Deliberate practice is distinguished from intentional repetition, requiring specific performance targets, feedback and opportunity for correction.
The series is set up around six questions, from what expertise is to how it might be recognised or measured.
quotes: Teaching shapes our chances in life, social mobility, health, participation in democratic life, and access to knowledge (knowledge begets knowledge).

Yet for something so important, teacher expertise is still surprisingly vague in much of our thinking about education. It's often under-defined, inconsistently described, and insufficiently supported in both policy and professional development.
All too often, expertise is confused with experience. In many other professions, this would be absurd.
A central claim of our book is that teaching expertise sits at the intersection of science and craft.
Expert teachers differ from experienced teachers because they don't merely accumulate experience; they systematically and deliberately learn from it, improving their practice.

Deliberate practice isn't simply intentionally practising something or doing more of the job. It's focused, effortful work aimed at improving specific aspects of performance, guided by feedback and opportunities for correction.
Striving for expertise in teaching isn't merely a personal ambition; it's a professional responsibility.
